schema_metadata.title: Search engine
schema_metadata.description: Full-detail structured knowledge graph based on the user-provided Wikipedia article about web search engines, including definitions, history, architecture, ranking, market context, bias, engine types, historical systems, and explicit relationships.

source_basis.primary_source: User-provided Wikipedia article text titled 'Search engine'
source_basis.scope_note: The supplied text is the source of the historical statements and figures below. Time-sensitive market-share figures are retained with their source date rather than represented as current.

entities.name: Search engine
entities.definition: A search application that responds to a user's query with links to web pages and other relevant information, often shown with snippets, images, and specialized result types.
entities.scope_note: This record focuses primarily on Internet and World Wide Web search, as in the supplied article.

entities.name: Information retrieval
entities.definition: The process of finding information relevant to a user's information need from a collection of documents or records.

entities.name: World Wide Web
entities.definition: A linked information system whose pages and resources can be discovered and accessed over the Internet.

entities.name: Search query
entities.definition: A word, combination of words, phrase, or sentence submitted to a search system.

entities.name: Search engine results page
entities.definition: A result interface containing ranked links and commonly snippets, images, and other result modules.

entities.name: Web crawler
entities.definition: Automated software that visits web resources, discovers links, and collects information for indexing.

entities.name: robots.txt
entities.definition: A conventionally named file containing directives that communicate crawl preferences to automated crawlers.

entities.name: Indexing
entities.definition: Associating words and other tokens from documents with locations, fields, and other searchable representations, then storing those associations in an index.

entities.name: Inverted index
entities.definition: An index structure mapping terms to documents or locations in which they occur.

entities.name: Search ranking
entities.definition: Ordering candidate results by estimated relevance or other ranking signals.

entities.name: Search result snippet
entities.definition: A short extract or description showing context relevant to a query.

entities.name: Search cache
entities.definition: Stored page content or representations retained to support retrieval and result processing between crawler visits.

entities.name: Link analysis
entities.definition: Analysis of hyperlinks among pages to infer relationships, relevance, authority, or importance.

entities.name: PageRank
entities.definition: A link-analysis algorithm associated with Google that uses the linking structure of the web to estimate page importance.

entities.name: RankDex
entities.definition: A site-scoring and ranking algorithm developed by Robin Li that used hyperlinks to assess the quality of indexed websites.

entities.name: Search advertising
entities.definition: Advertising associated with search queries or search result pages; commercial search engines may derive substantial revenue from advertising.

entities.name: Search engine optimization
entities.definition: Practices intended to improve a website's visibility in organic search results.

entities.name: Search engine bias
entities.definition: Ways search results and visibility may be shaped by indexing coverage, ranking methods, commercial incentives, geography, language, policy, personalization, or other system choices.

entities.name: Filter bubble
entities.definition: The hypothesis or concern that personalization and selection systems can narrow the information encountered by a user.

entities.name: Local search
entities.definition: Search focused on geographically relevant businesses, places, services, or information.

entities.name: Vertical search
entities.definition: Search focused on a specific subject area, content type, or industry.

entities.name: Metasearch engine
entities.definition: A search system that queries or aggregates results from multiple other search services.

entities.name: Enterprise search
entities.definition: Search across information belonging to an organization, company, government, or other enterprise.

entities.name: Multimedia search
entities.definition: Search across images, video, audio, or other non-text media.

entities.name: Semantic search
entities.definition: Search that attempts to use meaning, concepts, or relationships in addition to literal keyword matching.

entities.name: Voice search
entities.definition: Search initiated through spoken input or voice interfaces.

entities.name: Human-curated web directory
entities.definition: A categorized collection of web resources selected or organized by people rather than exclusively through automated crawling.

entities.name: Memex
entities.definition: Vannevar Bush's 1945 vision of a personal information retrieval system for navigating a large body of connected knowledge and annotations.

entities.title: As We May Think
entities.topic_role: Historical precursor to ideas about personal information retrieval and linked annotations.

entities.name: Vannevar Bush
entities.role_in_topic: Proposed the Memex concept in 1945.

entities.name: Alan Emtage
entities.role_in_topic: Created Archie, an early searchable index of file names from public anonymous FTP sites.

entities.name: Mark McCahill
entities.role_in_topic: Created Gopher in 1991, which was followed by search utilities including Veronica and Jughead.

entities.name: Oscar Nierstrasz
entities.role_in_topic: Wrote Perl scripts that mirrored and standardized web resource pages, forming the basis for W3Catalog.

entities.name: Matthew Gray
entities.role_in_topic: Created the World Wide Web Wanderer and the Wandex index in 1993.

entities.name: Jonathon Fletcher
entities.role_in_topic: Created JumpStation in December 1993.

entities.name: Michael Mauldin
entities.role_in_topic: Developed the Lycos search engine at Carnegie Mellon University in 1994.

entities.name: Robin Li
entities.role_in_topic: Developed RankDex and later used its technology in Baidu.

entities.name: Larry Page
entities.role_in_topic: Google co-founder associated with PageRank; his patent cited Robin Li's earlier RankDex work.

entities.name: Sergey Brin
entities.role_in_topic: Google co-founder and co-author of the 1998 paper describing a large-scale hypertext search engine.

entities.name: Jerry Yang
entities.role_in_topic: Co-founded Yahoo! with David Filo.

entities.name: David Filo
entities.role_in_topic: Co-founded Yahoo! with Jerry Yang.

entities.name: Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency
entities.role_in_topic: Historical sponsor of the Memex domain-specific search research program, mentioned in the related context.

entities.name: Google
entities.role_in_topic: Became the dominant global search provider in the 2000s, according to the supplied article.

entities.name: Microsoft
entities.role_in_topic: Developed its own crawling and search technology and launched Bing in 2009.

entities.name: Yahoo!
entities.role_in_topic: Began as a human-curated web directory and later operated search services powered by external and acquired technologies.

entities.name: Baidu
entities.role_in_topic: Chinese search provider founded by Robin Li; launched in 2000.

entities.name: Yandex
entities.role_in_topic: Search provider associated with Russia and listed among major engines in the article.

entities.name: DuckDuckGo
entities.role_in_topic: Search provider listed among active engines in the article's historical timeline.

entities.name: Brave
entities.role_in_topic: Search provider listed in the article's 2020s timeline.

entities.name: Naver
entities.role_in_topic: Search provider active in South Korea.

entities.name: Lycos
entities.role_in_topic: Search engine developed at Carnegie Mellon University in 1994.

entities.name: Excite
entities.role_in_topic: One of the early major commercial web search engines.

entities.name: AltaVista
entities.historical_status: Inactive; the article says it was acquired by Yahoo! in 2003 and later redirected to Yahoo!.

entities.name: Inktomi
entities.role_in_topic: Provided search technology used by Yahoo! and Microsoft/MSN Search during earlier phases.

entities.name: GoTo.com
entities.role_in_topic: The article says Google adopted the idea of selling search terms from this company in 1998.

entities.name: Archie
entities.scope: Public anonymous FTP file and directory names
entities.indexing_method: Downloaded FTP directory listings and created a searchable database of filenames; did not index file contents.

entities.name: Veronica
entities.expansion: Very Easy Rodent-Oriented Net-wide Index to Computerized Archives
entities.relationship_note: Searched keyword matches across Gopher menu listings.

entities.name: Jughead
entities.expansion: Jonzy's Universal Gopher Hierarchy Excavation And Display

entities.name: W3Catalog
entities.method: Periodically mirrored manually maintained resource pages and standardized them with Perl scripts.

entities.name: Wandex
entities.purpose: Index generated to estimate the size of the World Wide Web.

entities.name: World Wide Web Wanderer
entities.purpose: Measure the size of the Web; captured URLs.

entities.name: ALIWEB
entities.method: Relied on site administrators to submit index files; did not use a web robot.

entities.name: JumpStation
entities.limitation: Limited resources restricted indexing primarily to page titles and headings.

entities.name: WebCrawler
entities.capability: One of the first crawler-based all-text search engines; enabled searching for any word in a web page.

entities.name: RankDex
entities.capability: Used hyperlinks to measure the quality of indexed websites.

entities.name: Google Search
entities.historical_note: Rose to prominence around 2000, combining link-analysis ranking with a minimalist interface.

entities.name: Yahoo! Search
entities.historical_note: Initially searched Yahoo! Directory; later used external search technologies and acquisitions.

entities.name: MSN Search
entities.historical_note: Initially used Inktomi results, with later transitions through other sources and Microsoft's own crawler.

entities.name: Bing
entities.historical_note: Rebranded from Live Search; Yahoo! and Microsoft finalized a deal for Yahoo! Search to be powered by Bing technology in July 2009.

entities.name: Baidu Search
entities.historical_note: The article connects its technology to Robin Li's RankDex work.

entities.name: AI-powered search
entities.definition: Search experiences that integrate language models or other AI systems with search indexes to produce conversational answers, summaries, and contextual recommendations.
entities.article_context: The supplied article says this integration became increasingly common in the 2020s.

definition_and_core_functions.definition: A search application that accepts a query and provides links to web pages and other relevant information, commonly with snippets, images, and specialized result types.
definition_and_core_functions.provider_architecture: A search engine can be one component of a distributed computing system spanning multiple data centers.

core_tasks.name: Find and select content
core_tasks.description: Discover full or partial content relevant to query terms.

core_tasks.name: Maintain an index
core_tasks.description: Store searchable representations and references to document locations.

core_tasks.name: Search the index
core_tasks.description: Match user queries against the index and return candidate documents.

core_tasks.name: Rank results
core_tasks.description: Order candidate results according to relevance and other system-specific signals.

core_tasks.name: Render results
core_tasks.description: Generate a results page with links, snippets, and potentially images or specialized modules.

definition_and_core_functions.important_distinction: A user query usually searches the search engine's index, not the live Web in its entirety.

processes.name: Web crawling
operations: follow links according to crawl policy
limitations: Some content is inaccessible to crawlers.
Crawl budgets and policies prevent exhaustive crawling of every reachable page.
Infinite URL spaces, spider traps, spam, and other practical issues constrain crawling.
Some sites are crawled extensively while others are only partially crawled.

processes.name: Indexing
operations: associate tokens with URLs or domain names
store searchable associations in index structures
update the index as pages change

processes.name: Query processing
operations: apply query operators and filters where supported
combine signals needed to rank results

processes.name: Ranking
processes.caveat: Ranking methods differ by engine and change over time; commercial implementations may treat parts of their methods as trade secrets.

processes.name: Result rendering
operations: render specialized result types when available

processes.name: Cache and refresh management
operations: retain some page content or renderable representations
serve stored representations between crawler visits
refresh data according to crawl schedules and policies
processes.caveat: A cached representation may differ from the live page if the page has changed since it was crawled.

robots_exclusion.function: Communicates crawl directives to compliant crawlers.
robots_exclusion.limitation: Crawl directives do not guarantee that all content is indexed or that every crawler will behave identically.

features: concept-based or statistically informed search in some systems
query_refinement.user_feedback_loop: Users refine queries and filters after reviewing initial results.

ranking_and_relevance.goal: Present useful, relevant, or authoritative results early in the result list.
signals_described_in_article: freshness or modification time where used

rankdex.claim: The article describes RankDex as an early search ranking system using hyperlinks to measure website quality.
rankdex.historical_significance: The article says RankDex preceded Google's similar PageRank patent filing and that Robin Li later used the technology in Baidu.

pagerank.principle: Uses the linking structure of the Web and the PageRank of linking pages to estimate relative importance.
pagerank.article_reported_influence: Larry Page's patent cited Robin Li's earlier RankDex work.

tradeoffs: Relevance is not identical to popularity.
Index coverage limits what can be retrieved.
Different engines can produce different results because they use different indexes and ranking algorithms.
Ranking methods and user-facing behavior evolve over time.

pre_web_precursors.description: The article states that Internet user-search systems predate the Web and dates WHOIS search to 1982.
The article dates an early multi-network user-search service to 1989.
A vision for navigating and annotating a large body of connected information.

early_search_system_details.name: Archie
early_search_system_details.details: Downloaded public anonymous FTP directory listings and indexed filenames, not the contents of the files.

early_search_system_details.name: Veronica
early_search_system_details.details: Keyword search over Gopher menu titles.

early_search_system_details.name: Jughead
early_search_system_details.details: Retrieved menu information from specific Gopher servers.

early_search_system_details.name: W3Catalog
early_search_system_details.details: Standardized mirrored pages of manually maintained web resource catalogs.

early_search_system_details.name: World Wide Web Wanderer
early_search_system_details.details: Captured URLs; the article notes that URLs alone often did not provide descriptive information useful for searchers.

early_search_system_details.name: ALIWEB
early_search_system_details.details: Depended on webmasters to submit index files in a specified format.

early_search_system_details.name: JumpStation
early_search_system_details.details: Combined a crawler, index, and query interface but initially had limited fields available for indexing.

search_engine_types.description: Uses automated software agents to visit websites, read page content and metadata, follow links, and build or refresh an index.
Depends on people submitting or categorizing resources; only submitted or curated resources are included in the resulting collection.
examples: Yahoo! Directory as a historical precursor
limitations: coverage depends on submissions and editorial effort

search_engine_types.description: Combines automated crawling/indexing with human submissions, curation, or other sources.
Searches textual content using keywords, phrases, and sometimes limited natural-language queries.
Accepts spoken queries, typically through an assistant or voice interface.
examples: Yahoo! as listed in supplied article

search_engine_types.description: Searches media using visual appearance or other media-specific representations.
Supports questions expressed in restricted or natural language and returns answers or answer-oriented resources.
examples: NSIR as listed in supplied article

search_engine_types.description: Groups or clusters results to help users explore related topics.
Searches academic or scientific literature and may attempt to extract research concepts or findings.
examples: Nutch as listed in supplied article

search_engine_types.description: Focuses on a specific domain, subject, or content type.
Searches structured data, databases, or organization-specific repositories.
Aggregates or forwards queries to other search systems.
Integrates retrieval with AI-generated summaries or conversational answers.

historical_share_snapshot.precision_note: The source text gives approximate ranges or rounded figures; Google is represented as 89.5 only to encode the article's approximate 89–90% range, not as a precise independently verified measurement.
historical_share_snapshot.article_claim: May 2025 marked the first time in over a decade that Google's share fell below 90%.
historical_share_snapshot.freshness_warning: Historical snapshot only; not current market share.

commercial_model.history_note: The article says selling search terms, adopted by Google in 1998 from GoTo.com, contributed to the profitability of the search business.
commercial_model.ecosystem_effect: Website optimization historically focused heavily on Google because of its market share.

competition_and_consolidation: Search engines competed through result quality, index coverage, interface design, distribution deals, acquisitions, and monetization.
The article describes search providers entering the market during the late-1990s investment boom and some later withdrawing consumer products or changing focus.
The dot-com bubble peaked in March 2000, according to the supplied article.

russia.context: The article contains a dedicated section on search-engine market share in Russia.

east_asia.context: The article contains regional discussion of search in China, Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan, including the roles of local providers and changes in market use.
east_asia.caution: Regional market figures in the supplied article have their own dates and should not be treated as current without fresh verification.

search_engine_bias.article_context: The supplied article discusses research on coverage bias, search politics, representation of topics, and the effect of ranking systems on what users see.

customized_results_and_filter_bubbles.description: The article describes concerns that personalization and ranking can shape the information users encounter.
customized_results_and_filter_bubbles.evidence_caution: The existence and magnitude of filter-bubble effects are debated in the research literature; this schema records the topic as discussed, not a universal causal conclusion.

religious_search_engines.description: The article discusses specialized search services that filter or frame results for religious audiences.
religious_search_engines.caution: Examples are preserved as historical references from the article; current availability and operation are not asserted.

privacy_and_governance_topics: Search query data can be relevant to privacy analysis.
Search ranking and content moderation can raise governance questions.
Regional legal or policy requirements can affect result availability.

local_search.purpose: Find geographically relevant businesses, places, and services.
local_search.source_note: The supplied article includes a dedicated local-search section and a reference on local SEO.

search_engine_submission.description: Submitting a site or sitemap can be part of discovery workflows, but the article cites warnings that third-party search-engine submission services can be harmful.
search_engine_submission.caution: Submission does not guarantee crawling, indexing, ranking, or visibility.

social_bookmarking.description: The article compares search engines with social bookmarking and cites research asking whether social bookmarking can improve web search.

scientific_search.description: Scientific search engines index research literature; some research aims to extract theoretical constructs or key findings from articles.

search_advertising.description: Search advertising associates paid promotion with search terms or results; the article describes its importance to the commercial search business.

relationship_graph.node_id_convention: Stable string IDs are used for concepts, processes, people, companies, algorithms, and historical engines.
